content: Sudafed is a trademarked brand of over-the-counter (OTC) decongestants produced by Pfizer Inc. It is available in the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia, and Canada. The name Sudafed originates from its active ingredient, pseudoephedrine hydrochloride, which has traditionally been the key component of the product. However, due to legal restrictions on the sale of pseudoephedrine in many regions, some Sudafed products no longer contain pseudoephedrine. In late 2004, Pfizer announced the introduction of a new product called Sudafed PE, which replaced pseudoephedrine with phenylephrine as the active decongestant. Phenylephrine had already been used in other formulations for years. By 2005, Pfizer transitioned many of its decongestant products to phenylephrine, although the original pseudoephedrine-based Sudafed remained available. This shift was driven by increasing legal restrictions on pseudoephedrine due to its role as a precursor in the illicit production of methamphetamine, a highly addictive stimulant commonly referred to as crystal meth. Pfizer and its predecessor, Warner-Lambert, had explored alternative formulations to address regulatory concerns. In 1996, the company began testing a patented decongestant known as minus pseudoephedrine. This modified version reportedly provided sinus relief comparable to the original plus pseudoephedrine but could not be chemically converted into methamphetamine. Despite promising results in animal studies, Pfizer did not bring this ingredient to market due to the high costs and lengthy process required for regulatory approval. Additionally, Pfizer invested $12 million in developing additives for Sudafed that would make it more difficult to extract pseudoephedrine for illicit purposes. However, this project was abandoned in 2003, seven years after its inception. According to Dr. L. Hendeles from the University of Florida, the most commonly used decongestants are phenylpropanolamine, pseudoephedrine, and phenylephrine. While all three are sympathomimetic amines, their effectiveness varies. Phenylephrine, in particular, undergoes significant first-pass metabolism, which reduces its bioavailability at standard recommended doses. However, doses of 20 mg appear to be safe and may provide greater decongestant effects, as suggested by anecdotal evidence. In Australia, Sudafed products containing up to 60 mg of pseudoephedrine are available either by prescription or through a pharmacist. If a driver's license is not provided, pharmacists may still choose to dispense the medication at their discretion.
